title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Delete Cloud Instance
shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Delete Cloud Instance
summary: Deleting a cloud instance is a destructive cleanup step rather than a stealth one. Once the adversary has finished with a machine, terminating it removes the guest operating system, its event logs, its memory contents, and any files staged on its disks, unless those disks are detached or snapshots exist elsewhere. The same reasoning applies to attacker-created instances that were only ever a temporary workbench. In practice this behaviour produces a distinctive audit trail: an instance creation, a short or unusual lifetime, and a termination call, all attributed to one identity and often from a single source address. The defensive concern is that the deletion may be authorised and routine-looking, so the evidence of the intrusion has to come from sources outside the deleted machine, principally cloud control plane logs, network flow records, identity provider sign-in logs, and copies of log data forwarded to a central store before deletion. Where deletion is suspected, checking whether the machine had log forwarding enabled, whether it held unencrypted data, and whether any snapshots survive determines what can still be recovered. Alerting on termination of instances that are not in the change record, or on delete events from a new address or role, separates malicious cleanup from decommissioning.

beginner.definition: This technique is about an attacker shutting down and removing a cloud virtual machine. They often do this after using the machine for their own work. The deletion destroys the machine files, including many records of what happened on it. The attacker hopes the trail ends there with nothing left to examine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Logs and files inside a deleted machine are usually gone for good. Without them, investigators may never learn how the attacker entered or what they took. This is why cloud evidence must be copied to a central store as it is created. If you rely only on data inside the machine, a single delete can remove your whole investigation. Deletion can also destroy real business systems by accident.
howItWorks: The attacker finishes their work on a cloud machine they own or created.
They issue a terminate command through the cloud console or interface.
The cloud service shuts the machine down and frees its resources.
The machine disks may be deleted with it, unless they were kept separately.
Local logs, memory contents, and temporary files are no longer available.
Only the cloud activity record of the deletion remains as evidence.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital that retires the entire night shift equipment after a serious mistake. The old machines, the paper notes and the recordings all leave in one van. Investigators arrive the next morning and find a clean, empty room. They can ask what was removed, but they can no longer examine it.
takeaways: Copy cloud logs to a central store as soon as they are made.
Keep snapshots and detached disks when you need to investigate.
Alert on machine deletions that no change record explains.

objectives: Explain what evidence disappears when a cloud instance is deleted.
Describe how deletion fits into an attackers cleanup sequence.
Identify the cloud audit events that record instance termination.
Explain why centralised log shipping matters for cloud investigations.
Suggest controls that protect against destructive instance deletion.
